articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend What I Built I built InterviewMate , an AI-powered mock interview assistant for students preparing for placements and internships. I built it for a friend who was struggling with interview preparation. They could study technical concepts and solve coding problems, but practicing an actual interview was difficult. They needed a way to practice answering questions, speaking clearly, and getting feedback without depending on another person every time. InterviewMate simulates a real interview. Users can upload their resume, select their target role and technical topics, and start a timed mock interview. The AI asks questions based on their resume and selected topics, and users can answer by typing or speaking.

articles.title: Realtime Optimistic Updates and WebRTC Reconciliation for Consultation Session Failures
articles.excerpt: Short answer: a video consultation room should apply optimistic updates only to reversible interface state, tag every mutation with a scoped session token and idempotency key, and reconcile against an…
articles.body: Short answer: a video consultation room should apply optimistic updates only to reversible interface state, tag every mutation with a scoped session token and idempotency key, and reconcile against an authoritative room log after any disconnect. WebRTC can carry low-latency presence and cursor traffic, but it should not turn an unconfirmed clinical action into a fact. The uncomfortable trade-off is deliberate: cursors may briefly jump after reconnection; consent, appointment status, and clinician notes must never be guessed. This is a trust-boundary problem disguised as a latency problem. A patient can reasonably trust the local mute icon to react at once. They cannot reasonably be told that consent was recorded merely because one browser changed color.

articles.title: 10 Best Self-Hosted On-Call Scheduling Tools
articles.excerpt: Cross-posted from the Fluidify blog. Disclosure: I build FluidifyAI Regen, one of the tools below. If you're looking for a commercial, proprietary on-call tool you can run on your own infrastructure,…
articles.body: Cross-posted from the Fluidify blog . Disclosure: I build FluidifyAI Regen, one of the tools below. If you're looking for a commercial, proprietary on-call tool you can run on your own infrastructure, the answer is that almost none exist. PagerDuty, Opsgenie, incident.io, xMatters, and most of the category are SaaS-only, no on-premise license at any price. The tools that do run on your own infrastructure are, with rare exception, open source, so "self-hosted" and "open-source" end up covering nearly the same ground here. So this list only asks one question: how good is each tool at the scheduling job (rotation types, overrides, calendar sync, timezones), and what does it take to run and back up yourself.

articles.title: RocketMQ-Rust: route discovery is only the first connectivity check
articles.excerpt: A small debugging note from RocketMQ-Rust’s architecture docs: NameServer returns topic routes: Broker addresses and queue metadata. In a direct-client deployment, producers and consumers then communi…
articles.body: A small debugging note from RocketMQ-Rust’s architecture docs: NameServer returns topic routes: Broker addresses and queue metadata. In a direct-client deployment, producers and consumers then communicate with the Broker. Message storage and delivery belong to the Broker. That distinction matters when a client can fetch a route but still cannot send or consume. A successful NameServer request only confirms discovery worked. It does not prove the advertised Broker address is reachable from that client, or that the Broker can accept writes. A useful first check: compare the Broker address returned in the route with the network the client actually runs in. Then investigate Broker connectivity and write readiness separately. The architecture documentation explains these boundaries.

articles.title: Lanterns Season 1 Finale Review & Recap
articles.excerpt: Though most of the twists can be seen coming well in advance, Lanterns Episode 8 manages to wrap up the season on an emotionally satisfying note.
articles.body: Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Lanterns Season 1, Episode 8! How much you enjoy the finale of Lanterns Season 1 is going to depend heavily on how well you can manage your expectations. There have been plenty of outlandish fan theories regarding where the series has been building towards and the identity of Hal Jordan’s killer. Is Hal even dead, or is this all part of some massive conspiracy involving complex doppelganger constructs or Manhunter-based resurrection? Well, it’s best to put all of that to the side and just enjoy the finale for what it is. It’s probably not going to shock most of us with its plot twists and character developments. Nor does it represent a pivot back to the sort of spectacle we saw in Episode 5.
